title: Abstraction costs
subtitle: Choose the work your program performs

lessons.title: One pass, no temporary vector
lessons.task: Sum the squares of the even input values as i64, without collecting an intermediate vector.
lessons.hint: Filter references, widen before multiplying, and sum.
body: Iterator adapters construct a computation; consumers drive it. A filter-map-fold chain can process each element without materializing intermediate Vec values.

Static iterator types let the optimizer inline and combine operations. Zero-cost abstraction means you need not pay extra abstraction overhead compared with equivalent manual code; it does not mean the computation is free or always optimized identically.
The first step removes intermediate storage. The second makes short-circuiting visible by counting how many inputs are visited.

steps.title: Stop when the answer is known
steps.task: Return whether target exists and the number of visited items, stopping at the first match.
steps.hint: Use inspect to count visits and any to short-circuit.
body: Short-circuiting can save more work than a small instruction-level improvement. Avoid eager collect when you need only the first answer; keep observable side effects out of production iterator pipelines unless their order is intentional.

lessons.title: Specialize the hot path
lessons.task: Implement total for any T: Cost by summing cost() over the borrowed slice.
lessons.hint: Use the Cost method through each element.
body: A generic function can be compiled into concrete versions for its used types. This monomorphization gives the optimizer a concrete method implementation, enabling inlining and specialization of surrounding code.
The tradeoff is code size and compilation work. Many concrete instantiations may increase instruction-cache pressure. Inlining is an optimization choice, not a Rust language guarantee.
Implement one generic aggregation function and exercise it with two types. There is no need to heap-allocate either implementation.

lessons.title: Pay for flexibility deliberately
lessons.task: Apply each borrowed operation in order to the input.
lessons.hint: Fold over the slice and call apply on each trait object.
body: &dyn Trait pairs a data pointer with metadata used for dynamic dispatch. Different concrete implementors can share one interface at runtime. The indirect call may limit inlining, although compilers can sometimes devirtualize it.
Dynamic dispatch does not inherently require a heap allocation: &dyn Trait borrows existing storage. Box<dyn Trait> adds owning indirection, usually with heap storage for a non-zero-sized value.
Choose dynamic dispatch for heterogeneous collections or runtime selection; measure the actual workload before replacing a clear design with generics.
